title: Exploiting a centrally powered coherent microcomb for lightweight optical transmission

paper_content.abstract: The exponential growth of data capacity in intelligent terminals drives higher data traffic toward network edges. Compact I/O systems are essential to support space-constrained infrastructures at the computing edges or modular data centers. However, scaling high-capacity transmission via increasing physical channels is constrained by limited source coherence and low carrier-to-noise ratios (OCNR), hindering lightweight, efficient applications like distributed edge computing. Here, we exploit an integrated self-injection-locked dark-pulse microcomb to achieve 1 Tbps/λ/core transmission and characterize the constraints among OCNR, linewidth, and transmission rate. Furthermore, a multi-dimensional transmission architecture for multi-nodes aggregation is explored, boosting the transmission rate to 200 Tbps with 16 comb lines at 70 Gbaud. Combining with integrated waveshapers and semiconductor optical amplifiers, a chip-level parallel carrier generator is explored, reducing system size a hundredfold while delivering 5 Tbps. Our results highlight significant potential for compact and resource-conserving transmission systems in data centers and distributed high performance computing applications.
paper_content.introduction:
With the explosive growth of artificial intelligence (AI) and the internet of things (IoT) 1, the demand for efficient data transmission within the network has reached unprecedented levels. In addition to backbone network communications, the devices at the network edges, required to perform real-time monitoring 2 and high accuracy sensing 3, are also expected to simultaneously transmit massive information across distributed nodes or back to the data center for system coordination 4. Recent advances in optical cloud computing architectures have demonstrated significant potential for enabling AI workload offloading to edge networks 5, with experimental validation confirming seamless integration between distributed edge nodes and centralized cloud computing infrastructure across metropolitan-area optical networks. To meet these challenges, compact data links with lightweight infrastructures capable of supporting high throughput have become more essential 6.

Integrated photonics can provide high-density data link solutions. Despite the achievement of ultra-high capacity integrated parallel transmission systems, conventional schemes still struggle to deliver the required data throughput while maintaining compact structure and energy efficiency in space-limited and power-constrained scenarios. The challenges stem from two main aspects. Firstly, it is difficult for wavelength-division multiplexing (WDM) parallel light sources to obtain both low noise and compact forms simultaneously. While distributed feedback (DFB) laser diode arrays have been commercially successful 7,8, they exhibit limited phase noise and complexity in synergistic frequency control. Quantum dot mode-locked lasers 9–13 can generate multiple channels with a single laser diode, but the inherent high phase noise reduces the maximum transmission rate for coherent communication. Other integrated multiwavelength sources, such as electro-optical combs 14–16 and Kerr microcombs 17–21, relying on high-power, high-purity optical or microwave sources for low-noise wideband comb generation, which results in bulky and costly setups for edge nodes. Self-injection locked (SIL) Kerr microcombs offer high-coherent multiwavelength sources with a laser diode directly coupled to a high-quality optical nonlinear microcavity. However, the relatively low combline powers of microcombs degrade the OCNR with the optical amplification, limiting the data rates per channel. Optical-injection amplified combs 22,23 have been proposed to avoid the OCNR degeneration, while the employment of laser diode arrays hinders their application for lightweight systems.

Another issue lies in the subsequent system. As the channel count often spans multiple optical bands (S/C/L) for high-capacity integrated optical demonstrations, the link setup of each wavelength, comprising modulators, amplifiers, and passive couplers, grows dramatically in real-world deployments. This increase occurs not only due to the need to scale the same devices within each band 24, but also the differing design structures and operating principles required across bands 25. The use of excessive wavelengths in high-capacity transmission will further exacerbate nonlinear signal crosstalk, which may degrade overall signal quality and limit system throughput, particularly in tightly packed wavelength grids 26,27. Therefore, merely increasing the number of physical channels in the system makes it difficult to realize lightweight, cost-effective high-capacity signal transmission. To date, although achieves over 1 Pbps high-throughput transmission 28, wavelength resources are often underutilized, resulting in reduced communication conversion efficiency and increased device overhead.

Ideally, a compact transmission system at edge nodes needs a parallel light source covering a single band with high coherence and adequate OCNR. Such a source is essential to maximize single-channel capacity, enable multi-dimensional multiplexing for even higher aggregate rates, and tolerate the performance degradation inherent in lightweight systems.

In this work, we achieve high-capacity optical transmission and a streamlined system architecture by employing an integrated SIL comb source. The highly integrated source provides both high coherence with ~40 dB frequency noise suppression and high per-channel power with >60% on-chip conversion efficiency. Among 16 channels within the C-band, each channel exhibits an intrinsic linewidth below 600 Hz with power exceeding −10 dBm. To establish an overarching framework for our study, we perform a detailed investigation of the constraints among OCNR, linewidth, and achievable transmission rate. The experimental results indicate that a narrow linewidth <1 kHz is essential for elevated Gbaud single-channel transmission in our system, positioning the SIL microcomb as a key enabler of high-capacity lightweight systems. We experimentally demonstrated short-reach campus/edge networks and metropolitan area network transmission separately. In the campus/edge networks, we achieve a transmission capacity of 1 Tbps/λ across all carriers using a self-homodyne system. Furthermore, we perform multi-dimensional multiplexing by incorporating with WDM methods across various schemes, such as spatial mode, linear polarization (LP) mode, and orbital angular momentum (OAM), with the highest baud rate in comb-based transmission at 70 Gbaud. Specifically, in the WDM-spatial division multiplexing (SDM) scheme, the maximum transmission capacity exceeds 200 Tbps using only 16 high-quality comb carriers in the C-band. This reduces both wavelength resource requirements and channel count by more than ten times compared to previous demonstrations with the same capacity. Finally, for more compact deployment scenarios, a chip-level multicarrier generator is demonstrated, replacing bulky erbium-doped fiber amplifiers (EDFAs) and wavelength-selective switches (WSS) with integrated semiconductor optical amplifiers and silicon photonic waveshapers. Contributing to the original narrow linewidth and high OCNR, optical carriers provided by the SIL microcomb can tolerate the higher noise figures and insertion losses of integrated devices. The proposed scheme shrinks the system size by a hundredfold with an aggregation rate of 5 Tbps. By fully exploiting the integrated parallel high-coherence optical carriers, the proposed transmission scheme paves the way for high-capacity, ultra-lightweight solutions in next-generation edge computing networks (Fig. 1).
paper_content.results:
Lightsource effects on transmission system
To fulfill the demand for a compact, highly coherent source, the SIL microcomb scheme is implemented for frequency noise compression and carrier-to-noise enhancement in this work, as shown in Fig. 2b. A laser diode chip, which exhibits a wall-plug efficiency of 13.45%, is directly coupled with the designed silicon nitride (SiN) microresonator chip. The output spectrum from the laser chip through the SiN chip to the fiber link is given in Fig. 2a, with the output wavelength around 1555.37 nm and the output power of 14.86 dBm. Considering the laser diode direct output power of 18 dBm, the total optical insertion loss is estimated as 3.14 dB. The SiN microresonator consists of a rectangular waveguide with a height of 300 nm and a width of 3 μm for both high-quality and normal dispersion conditions. Figure 2c shows one of the measured resonances around 1555.37 nm, where the loaded quality factor is measured as 1.7×10⁷. Such high quality factor is significant for microcomb generation with limited optical power without amplification, and for noise suppression with self-injection locking. In this way, both frequency noise and spontaneous emission noise can be minimized. Figure 2d exhibits the generated coherent microcomb. Thanks to the normal dispersion condition, the spectrum is highly concentrated within C-band with high conversion efficiency. For adequate OCNR, we select the central 16 comblines with power exceeding −10 dBm as parallel optical carriers. The on-chip conversion efficiency from the pump laser to the 15 generated comblines (excluding the residual pump laser) is calculated to be 61.5%, with the center 16 high-power comblines accounting for ~99.7% of the converted energy. In addition, the frequency noise of the generated comblines is lower than the free-running laser, where the noise is suppressed by ~40 dB for the pump laser. Due to the repetition rate fluctuation, the combline coherence degenerates as apart from the pump laser. Owing to the self-injection locking, all 16 comblines express the intrinsic linewidth below 600 Hz.

To quantitatively verify the necessity of such high-performance sources for high-capacity transmission, we conduct a systematic investigation of the impact of linewidth and OCNR on optical communication systems under back-to-back (BTB) conditions. The experimental link transmits DP-16QAM signals as described in the Methods, wherein a Keysight N7714A external cavity laser (ECL) with 10-kHz linewidth serves as the local oscillator (LO). Optical carrier linewidths are varied from 1 Hz to 10 MHz, provided by different commercial lasers and comb lines of the SIL microcomb. The OCNR is adjusted by controlling the laser intensity via a variable optical attenuator. Intuitively, high-speed transmission systems require coordinated optimization of both OCNR and laser linewidth characteristics. While the degradation of OCNR critically impacts transmission, light sources with superior coherence properties, could partially alleviate such degradation. With narrow linewidth (200 Hz for example), an OCNR of ~45 dB suffices to achieve transmission rate exceeding 100 GBaud, where a higher OCNR provides negligible improvement. Importantly, maintaining a linewidth <1 kHz is essential to achieve 1 Tbps in our system, as coherent receivers exhibit heightened sensitivity to phase noise under high-speed signal conditions. As coherence progressively deteriorates, the accumulated phase noise not only elevates the bit error rate (BER) at the receiver but also disrupts frequency offset estimation in the offline digital signal processing. This impairment leads to failed carrier phase recovery and ultimately complete system failure.

Parallel node-to-node data transfer
Currently implemented distributed edge computing systems primarily focus on short-reach campus/edge networks and metropolitan area network transmission, and avoid excessive hardware overhead to maintain edge computing capabilities. Thus, a high single-carrier capacity facilitates efficient data aggregation with minimal scaling requirements. To validate this, parallel wavelength multiplexing data transmission is performed, employing the central 16 comblines. The experimental setup is illustrated in Fig. 3a. SIL comb lines are divided into odd and even banks to simulate real-world communication scenarios. First, we build up a 1 km self-homodyne coherent transmission system to explore the maximum capacity of the comb lines. Limited by the channel spacing of 100 GHz, we artificially doubled the spectral interval through WSS, as shown in Fig. 3b, and distinguish the channels by their transparency. Thanks to the high OCNR with power levels above −10 dBm, all channels can support 110 GBaud DP-32QAM signal transmissions in the WDM configuration, indicating a single-channel rate of 1.1 (net 1.008) Tbps below the 9.1% forward error correction (FEC) threshold with a BER of 7×10⁻³.

Despite self-homodyne coherent system can support ultrahigh transmission rate, it is not suitable for metropolitan area network transmission, considering the requirements of precise fiber-length alignments and extra channels for LO transmission. Thus, the transmission results based on the homodyne coherent scheme are also provided in this section. The symbol rate is limited to 70 Gbaud due to constraints from the power level and linewidth characteristics of the edge comb lines, while simultaneously satisfying requirements for fiber transmission loss and component insertion losses. DP-16QAM signals are then modulated onto the parallel carriers, which are subsequently combined and transmitted through a 160-km standard single mode fiber (SMF). At the receiver end, the LO source and transmitted comb lines are detected and mixed by a coherent receiver. Overall, this 16-channel WDM scheme achieves a raw (net) aggregated rate of 8.96 (8.37) Tbps below the 7% hard decision (HD)-FEC BER threshold.

Extending beyond previous work showing minimal degradation from a soliton microcomb verses a 10kHz narrow-linewidth ECL 18, we demonstrate a substantial improvement in transmission quality by introducing the SIL scheme here. Figure 3d shows the error vector magnitude (EVM) results for each carrier in WDM transmission with DP formats. Compared with a high-performance tunable ECL1 with a ~10kHz linewidth (gray dots), the self-injection locking scheme (purple dots) exhibits a 3dB lower OSNR requirement at the same EVM level due to the high coherence. Figure 3e compares the ECL1 and the 1550.72nm combline (−6 channel) for 160-km transmission. The SIL comb with better noise performance delivers superior BER levels. The OSNR values at a BER of 3.8×10−3 are calculated for the −6, +6, −3, +3, and 0 channels and compared with ECL at the same wavelength, as illustrated in Fig. 3f. This comparison also validates the lower OSNR requirements for the narrower linewidth carriers. It also can be seen that the OSNR penalty difference between the referenced ECL carrier and the narrow-linewidth comb lines increases from 1dB at BTB transmission to 3dB after 160-km. This demonstrates during long-haul transmission, the pulse-like transmission format of the microcomb solution can better resist nonlinear distortions, potentially optimizing signal quality compared to traditional WDM schemes 29, hinting at superior performance compared to commercial ECLs.

Multi-dimensional transmission aggregation
SDM transmission over a field-deployed fiber has been practically demonstrated recently 30. Multiplexing dimensions 31, including spatial, LP mode, and OAM mode, hold promising prospects in next-generation edge networks. Such cascaded multiplexing schemes can aggregate information from distributed nodes operating with the same standardized wavelength configuration. Compared to continuously expanding the wavelength channels, this approach results in a more compact and cost-effective system architecture.

To simulate the aforementioned multi-node aggregation scenario, a 2-km 24-core multi-core fiber (MCF) with a mode field diameter of 9 μm was used. The crosstalk of 24-core MCF is ~28 dB for nearest neighbors, ~49 dB for next-nearest neighbors, and ~62 dB for next-next-nearest neighbors and beyond, as shown in Fig. 4b. In this case, we achieve a raw (net) transmission rate of 215.04 (200.97) Tbps below the 7% HD-FEC BER threshold by loading 70 Gbaud DP-16QAM signals, with only 16 wavelength channels, as shown in Fig. 4c. As far as we are aware, this represents the highest rate realized with an on-chip light source over the entire C-band, significantly simplifying the cumulative device requirements while avoiding saturation of the EDFAs.

Besides, we show the first proof-of-concept mode-division multiplexed (MDM) multi-dimensional transmission includes LP modes in a few-mode fiber (FMF) and OAM modes in a ring-core fiber (RCF) driven by the integrated photonic light source. Two modes are considered here for each scheme, where FMF supports the LP01 and LP02 and RCF supports OAM11 and OAM21, as shown in Fig. 4a. Nonlinear losses and crosstalk across all channels are measured in both schemes, as shown in Fig. 4d. Although higher-order modes exist more crosstalk, the fibers maintain inter-coupling below −15 dB, making them suitable for seamless linking with the front WDM for boosted capacity. Figure 4e shows the WMD-MDM transmission results for LP01 and LP02 mode carrying 40-Gbaud DP-16QAM signals transmitted over a 25-km FMF, with raw (net) capacity of 10.24 (9.57) Tbps. Compared to back-to-back transmission, MDM signals incur an additional OSNR penalty of ~6 dB after transmission over 25-km FMF. OAM modes are multiplexed and demultiplexed by a dedicated functional device 32 operating in C-band, with over 95% generating purity and <3 dB insertion loss. Similarly, the WDM-MDM transmission performance of 16 comb lines carrying 70-Gbaud SP-16QAM signals with raw (net) rate reaching 8.96 (8.37) Tbps in a 50-m RCF using OAM11 and OAM21 modes, as shown in Fig. 4f. It is observed that MDM transmission of OAM modes in this scenario brings about 8-dB OSNR penalty around 7% HD-FEC threshold, compared with BTB transmission. The results validate the feasibility of microcomb-based multi-dimensional cascaded multiplexing schemes using passive specialty fiber links, offering a budget-friendly solution without the need for additional wavelength-dependent active devices.

Highly integrated lightweight transmission
Under stringent cost and footprint constraints, bulky equipment impedes system integration, particularly for achieving lightweight transmission in distributed edge nodes. In this section, beyond integrated light sources, we present a chip-level parallel carrier generator where bulky WSSs and EDFAs are replaced by SOAs and silicon photonic integrated waveshaping chips (IWCs). Figure 5a illustrates the architecture of the chip-level transmitter module, with photographs of all modules provided in Fig. 5b. The IWC is fabricated using mature silicon photonics technology, featuring cascaded microring resonators with a free spectral range (FSR) of ~1.3 THz. Microheaters placed above the microrings allow tuning of resonant frequencies to adjust the output spectrum, as detailed in Supplementary Information Note 5. To suppress thermal crosstalk, adjacent microrings are physically separated by etched trenches, as illustrated in Fig. 5c. Since not all comb lines require power equalization, we achieve uniform power distribution across all spectral lines using only 12 microrings. After the IWC, all 16 comb lines are equalized to −18 dBm per carrier, accounting for an 8 dB insertion loss. All carriers are then amplified by an SOA to a total output power of 18 dBm and routed through another IWC for odd-even channel separation. The separated carriers are modulated by 35-GHz-bandwidth DP-IQ modulators (which introduce 20 dB of insertion loss), combined, and then amplified by an SOA to an output power of 2 dBm before transmission. As demonstrated in Fig. 5e, a 10-km transmission at 5.12 Tbps (net 5.015 Tbps, 5 channels under 7% HD-FEC threshold condition) is achieved using 40-GBaud DP-16QAM signals. The BER trend per channel aligns consistently with the linewidth values as shown in Fig. 5d, with comb lines below 300 Hz linewidth achieving error-free operation.

It is noteworthy that the capacity of the present chip-level transmitter is lower than that of systems based on bulky devices. This primarily stems from carrier performance degradation caused by integrated components, which feature higher noise figures and insertion losses than their benchtop counterparts. Specifically, the IWC contributes an additional 3 dB insertion loss compared to benchtop WSS. SOAs, while far more compact than EDFAs, introduce excessive amplified spontaneous emission (ASE) noise. Meanwhile, their high α-factor and nonlinear effects (notably XPM) further induce cumulative phase noise and waveform distortion in high-speed systems 33,34. Figure 5f presents the corresponding noise degradation after an SOA amplification. When amplified to 10 dBm, the linewidth of channel 6 increases by approximately threefold and tenfold via EDFA and SOA respectively. After two SOAs, IWC and modulators, the OCNR decreases by 13 dB at the 2 dBm output operating point, as shown in Fig. 5g. We find that when the input optical carrier has an OCNR < 25 dB, the ASE noise from the dual SOAs completely overwhelms the carrier, rendering it incapable of supporting signal transmission. Despite these impairments, the SIL light source still enables >5 Tbps transmission within the chip-level lightweight system, due to its original superior coherence and OCNR. For comparison, we implement a reference system using a 45-GHz-spacing electro-optic frequency comb pumped by an N7714A ECL (Fig. 5d). Under identical conditions, severely degraded constellation diagrams are obtained due to its poor original coherence (Fig. 5e black pentagrams).
paper_content.methods:
Detailed characterization of microcomb
The silicon nitride resonator was fabricated with a standard integrated photonic foundry process. A 300 nm silicon nitride layer (refractive index 1.95 @ 1550nm) is encapsulated by highly transparent silica cladding, with the bottom oxide layer thickness of 4.4 μm and the top oxide layer of 3.5 μm. The silicon substrate is 725 μm thick. To achieve low loss and adequate dispersion, the microresonator waveguide width was designed to be 3 μm, with the bus waveguide of 1 μm. The fabricated microresonator exhibits a free spectral range of 100 GHz (aligned with the DWDM ITU grid spacing standard), a Q-factor of ~1.7×10⁷, and a coupling loss of ≤2.5 dB/facet @ 1550nm. The microring resonator adopts a racetrack configuration, with Euler bends on both curved sections. The coupling gap is 1 μm, and the coupling length is 110 μm, forming an overall weakly overcoupled structure.

Our DFB laser outputs ~18 dBm, which is reduced to 14.86 dBm after traversing the microresonator. The DFB laser was mounted on a six-axis translation stage (Thorlabs MAX602D/M) and controlled by a benchtop laser diode driver (Thorlabs ITC4001). The SiN microresonator, maintained at room temperature, was placed on a three-axis translation stage (Thorlabs MAX313D). Alignment between the DFB laser and the SiN microresonator is achieved using a piezoelectric controller to adjust the six-axis stage. The output was collected by lensed fibers, with 1% of the light directed to an optical spectrum analyzer (Yokogawa AQ6370C) and the remaining 99% connected to subsequent communication systems or noise measurement setups. When the DFB laser diode was powered on, the current was set around 300 mA, and the temperature was maintained at ~30 °C. By fine-tuning the position of the six-axis stage, the generation of dark pulse soliton frequency combs can be observed on the optical spectrum analyzer (as shown in Fig. 2d). Stable microcomb generation is sustained for over 1000 min.

We employed delayed self-heterodyne interferometry to measure the spectral phase noise. The desired wavelength was filtered out using an optical filter. The signal was then split into two paths with equal power: one path was frequency-shifted by a 200 MHz acousto-optic modulator (AOM), while the other passed through a 10-km (10 m for MHz Laser) fiber delay line. Both paths were subsequently combined using a 2×2 50/50 optical coupler (OC) and directed to two photodetectors (PD). The output signals were captured by an oscilloscope at a sampling rate of 500 MSa/s, collecting 80 million data points, which were then processed using custom software.

Fabrication and characterization of the SDM (de)multiplexers
The optical fibers used in the experiments (a 160-km SMF, a 2-km 24-core MCF, a 25-km FMF and a 50-m RCF) are all provided by YOFC. We fabricate all the (de)multiplexers needed for SDM experiments. The 24-core MCF (de)multiplexer are self-made fan-in/fan-out 3D photonic devices based on femtosecond laser writing technology. The glass chip (dimension: 40 mm × 20 mm × 1 mm) is inscribed by a high repetition rate Ytterbium-based laser to form 24-channel (de)multiplexer. The measured insertion losses of (de)multiplexer are all lower than 1.5 dB in C band, with the maximum and minimum inter-channel crosstalk of −19.8 dB and −30.6 dB respectively. For LP modes (de)multiplexing, we employed all-fiber mode-selective couplers (MSCs) based on the side-polishing technique 47. The MSC consists of a SMF and a FMF. When the effective refractive index of the fundamental mode in the SMF matches that of the higher-order modes in the FMF, the fundamental mode is coupled into the FMF to generate the corresponding LP02 mode. The fundamental mode in the FMF maintains its mode nature as it passes through the MSC. As a result, the MSC successfully enables the multiplexing of the LP01 and LP02 modes. The LP multiplexer and demultiplexer are connected by an FMF to characterize their desirable performance. Across the entire C-band, they exhibit a loss of less than 1.5 dB and crosstalk of less than −15 dB. For OAM modes (de)multiplexing, we utilized MSCs similar to those used for LP mode (de)multiplexing 32. The difference lies in the use of the fused biconical taper technique for OAM modes (de)multiplexing. Additionally, a multimode fiber (MMF) is used instead of an FMF. Furthermore, we implemented two cascaded MSCs to achieve the multiplexing of OAM11 and OAM21 mode. The cascaded OAM multiplexer demonstrates a loss of less than 2.5 dB and crosstalk of less than −15 dB across the entire C-band.

Detailed coherent experimental setup
The experimental results presented in Fig. 2e were obtained using multiple light sources with varying linewidth characteristics: NKT Photonics (1 Hz), Comb 0 (25 Hz), Comb 1 (81.64 Hz), Comb 5 (220 Hz), SANTEC TSL-510 (1.576 kHz), RIO ORION-1550-30-15-M (5 kHz), KEYSIGHT N7714A ECL (10.4 kHz), ALNAIR TLT-200 (20 kHz), APEX AP3350A (238 kHz), and CONQUER CUSTOMIZED (628 kHz), along with two cases that failed demodulation-an InP DFB laser (3 MHz) and BOXOPTRONICS CUSTOMIZED (8.8 MHz). Throughout the transmission experiments, the KEYSIGHT N7714A ECL served as the LO to maintain phase reference stability. It must be emphasized that all OCNR measurements were performed with the optical spectrum analyzer’s resolution bandwidth set to 6.25 GHz.

In our work, we employed self-homodyne and homodyne coherent detection schemes for optical communication demonstration. The homodyne scheme modifies the self-homodyne setup by replacing LO path with an additional light source, while other configurations remain unchanged. Notably, for a WDM system with a single-wavelength rate of 1 Tbps, self-homodyne detection system demands precise alignment of the signal and LO path lengths, exhibiting a trend where lower linewidths of light source result in higher tolerance levels. At the transmitter, integrated comb chip generates 16 comb lines as the WDM channels while 16 ECLs are used to load channels for comparison experiment. The channel spacing of both solutions is 100 GHz. The WSS (Finisar Waveshaper 4000s) (with 5 dB insertion loss) splits these channels into odd/even paths. Subsequently, the light source carrying 16 wavelengths is amplified by an amplifier to boost the power of each channel, with the aggregate power reaching ~13 dBm prior to entering two 35-GHz 3 dB bandwidth IQ modulators (Sumicem T.SBXH1.5PL-35PD-ADC). Both paths are simultaneously modulated by data generated from a 128-GSa/s Arbitrary Waveform Generator (AWG-M9505A). Depending on the data rate, the output optical signal power varies within the range of −7 dBm to −14 dBm. The odd and even signals decorrelating by a 10-ns optical delay lines are coupled with similar power levels and fed into the transmission link. When transitioning to single-polarization transmission, only one polarization of the dual-polarization modulator is utilized, with the corresponding modulator drive voltage applied to that polarization. The modulator’s bias voltage is dynamically adjusted by an automatic bias controller to ensure stable high-speed signal performance and efficient operation.

The transmission link consists of an EDFA (KEOPSYS) for signal amplification, multiplexers/demultiplexers, and multidimensional multiplexing fiber to validate the optical comb’s transmission performance. The SDM channels are fully decorrelated to each other, with 10-ns optical delay lines between each channel. The power injected into the fiber is kept below 10 dBm to mitigate fiber nonlinear effects. At the receiver, amplification, filtering, attenuation and amplification scheme is employed for WDM demultiplexing and OSNR adjustment. The LO light, amplified to 18 dBm by an EDFA, is coherently detected with the signal light (around 0 dBm) by a dual-polarization coherent receiver consisting of a polarization-diversity 90-degree hybrid and four 70-GHz 3 dB bandwidth balanced photodiodes. A 256-GSa/s real-time oscilloscope (KEYSIGHT UXR0594AP) with 59-GHz bandwidth captures waveforms from four channels and sends them to a computer for DSP. In the context of DSP, at the transmitter side, we initially generate a PRBS sequence for QAM mapping, followed by 0.01 Root Raised Cosine pulse shaping, and then resample the signal before sending it to the AWG. On the receiver side, the captured signal undergoes sequential processing including resampling, frame synchronization, dispersion compensation, carrier frequency offset estimation using the fourth-power algorithm, adaptive MIMO equalization, carrier phase recovery through a two-stage blind phase search algorithm (with filter lengths of 32 and 8 for the first and second stages, respectively), demodulation, and BER calculation. It is noteworthy that during the verification of the relationship between OCNR and linewidth versus maximum net rate, DSP section utilized an 81-tap adaptive MIMO equalizer. In other experimental scenarios, the use of a 41-tap MIMO equalizer with reduced compensation capability and the decreased received OSNR per comb line caused by WDM collectively lead to a degradation in achievable symbol rate compared to the former configuration.

reviewer_comments.reviewer_1:
This paper presents the use of a self injection locked microcomb as a source for coherent optical fiber transmission in the C-band achieving a net rate of 8.4 Tbps in WDM scheme and a net 200 Tbps in a WDM + MCF configuration. Additionally, MDM transmissions are also demonstrated achieving net 9.57 and 8.37 Tbps. The authors claim a 10-fold reduction in resource requirements for similar capacity architectures. The paper is well organized but could improve in the following areas.

Please specify in more details the exact DSP that was used at both the transmitter and at the receiver. It would be interesting to know filter lengths, equalization and pre-emphasise used, etc.

The authors claim the first coherent single-lambda comb-based transmission results over 1 Tbps, however their citation [8] (Bernal S, et al.) includes a single-lambda demonstration of 1.6 Tbps in the O-band. Please adapt the claim accordingly.

The authors compare the performance of the comb lines vs commercial ECLs for different OSNR values. It would be valuable to add a discussion on the amount of gain needed in their proposed architecture since it requires more optical amplification than a single laser WDM scheme.

The authors claim their design is lightweight as it only uses one optical source, however their WDM transmission still requires 16 DP-IQMs, EDFAs, mux/demux, etc. to be integrated into the same chiplet. I recommend the authors carefully justify the full size of their proposed architecture. It would also be interesting to see a discussion on their proposed architecture being used in a bi-directional link.

The discussion section provides a good summary of the obtained results as compared to previous works but does not provide an impactful argument explaining why this type of comb source is ideal for their proposed architecture. A more detailed comparison between the limitations of this type of comb source compared to others would be of great interest. Additionally, system sensitivities to temperature would be of value to the study.

Other comments:
Please specify for all the throughput values if they are net (after FEC) or not.

In the Noise compression for ultra-high carrier capacity section, two laser output powers are mentioned. Please clarify which is the output of the laser diode and which is the output of the optical comb.

Please fix minor spelling errors such as “combine” instead of "comb line”.

Figure 2(g) shows two curves labeled 1 Tbps results each. It might be better to remove that label as every point on those curves does not equal a net 1 Tbps throughput.

In Parallel node-to-node data transfer, ECL1 and comb are both described as (gray dots) for Figure 3(b)
reviewer_comments.reviewer_2:
In this manuscript, “Exploiting a Centrally Powered Coherent Microcomb for Lightweight Optical Transmission” , the authors use the comb lines of a microcomb to demonstrate:
- 1 Tbps (115 GBd 32 QAM-DP) with one of the lines;
- 8.4 Tbit/s with 16 lines (70 GBd 16QAM-DP) over 160 km of SSMF;
- 200 Tbps with 16 lines (40 GBd 16QAM-DP) over 2 km of a 24-core fiber;
- 9.5 Tbps with 16 lines (40 GBd 16QAM-DP) over 25 km of a 2-mode (LP) fiber;
- 8.4 Tbps with 16 lines (70 GBd 16QAM-SP) over 50 m of a 2-mode (OAM) fiber.
The authors make use of such high symbol rates thanks to the low noise properties of each comb line, which is achieved by self-injection locking of the DFB pump laser. While the high on-chip conversion efficiency of 60% is associated with the type of comb.
The manuscript is clearly written, and the topic and results are relevant for the scientific community. My major concern relates to the novelty impact of this work. First, regarding the comb the authors employ, this seems to be the same as the one reported in Ref. 22, where the noise reduction is already analysed (as well as in other references) and the comb is already used for data transmission: 30 GBd, 32QAM-DP. The authors, thus need to clarify if this is the same comb and what is the main novelty with respect to that work. Otherwise, the work feels that it is an incremental enabled by using better components such as modulators and AWGs.

Second, when it comes to the 1 Tbps claim, this is shown only for one of the comb lines, i.e., the pump line. The authors should also characterize other lines in the same way (Fig. 2g). Will there be a penalty due to the lower power / higher noise? With only one line, their 1 Tbps is not that novel, see ,e.g., [Buchali, 1-Terabit/s Net Data-Rate Transceiver Based on Single-Carrier Nyquist-Shaped 124 Gbaud PDM-32QAM], or [First Single-Carrier Transmission at Net Data Rates of 1.6 Tb/s over 9075 km and 2.4 Tb/s over 1210 km Using 300 GBd Dual-Polarization Signals and Probabilistic Constellation Shaping].
If the selling point is to also demonstrate the high data rate with MCF, FMF, RCF, there has been already works bringing this approach tothe extrem: [22.9 Pb/s data-rate by extreme space-wavelength multiplexing] with a few-modes MCF providing 114 spatial channels (30 Tbps/wavelength).

Finally, the authors claim 200 tbps to be the highes with an integrated source, but already Ref.21 in 2018 showed 600 tbps, and maybe I am missing other examples.

In summary, the authors would need to position their work a bit more fairly and more clearly with respect to the state of the art in a meaningful way before the manuscript can be accepted.

Other comments:
- The manuscript, including methods and supplementary material, does not provide detailed description of: microresonator used (although I assume is the one from Ref 22), the soliton state, all equipment used, DSP, etc. The lack of details prevents properly evaluating the veracity of their results and questions its reproducibility.
- The authors highlight the power conversion efficiency, but what about the wall-plug efficiency? How does it compare to other similar approaches?
- The authors performed several transmission demonstrators with different symbol rates, modulation formats, with SMF, MCF, FMF, RCF. They could consider having a simple way to indicate them, e.g, table or in the respective figures.

Some typos:
-line 140: “combines”
- line 247 : “include”
- Line 293 “perabit”
- Line 252
Fig. 5 : this should be just for comb-based transmission experiments.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_3:
This manuscript reports technically work demonstrating high-speed multidimensional optical communication utilizing a self-injection-locked (SIL) dark-pulse microcomb. The authors ascribe the achieved high baud rate and 1 Tbps per-channel performance to the noise suppression facilitated by injection locking. However, in comparison with existing literature, this study does not introduce a fundamentally novel device architecture or a system-level innovation of transformative significance. Rather, the primary contribution appears to be the enhancement of single-carrier transmission rates, achieved at the cost of a reduced number of utilized channels, without providing substantial forward-looking perspectives. Consequently, I believe the scope and impact of this work might be more appropriately aligned with the focus of specialized journals in photonics or communications. The reasons I'm not entirely convinced by this work are listed below.

1. The authors attribute the high baud rate and 1 Tbps/channel performance to noise suppression via injection locking, but this claim lacks quantitative support.
(a) Please provide comparative data (OCNR, linewidth/phase noise, combline power) between the SIL and non-SIL combs. How do these differences translate to single-wavelength capacity?
(b) The explanation for setting the baud rate based on OCNR (lines 186-187) is unclear. What is the precise relationship between OCNR and maximum baud rate per channel? Why does the SIL comb achieve higher baud rates than other sources? Supporting analysis is required.
(c) The 1 Tbps record relies on a single high-power comb line. This does not represent the system's parallel performance and weakens the claim of a system-level breakthrough based on the microcomb.

2. The authors frequently emphasize the "lightweight" nature of the system, attributed to the compactness and conversion efficiency of the SIL comb.
(a) However, reliance on external EDFA amplification and WSSs for spectral shaping/equalization (Supplementary Note 4) contradicts the compactness claim. The authors should propose mitigation strategies or quantify the hardware overhead.
(b) Furthermore, the use of EDFAs and WSSs may negate the noise benefits of SIL combs. How does ASE noise impact OCNR, linewidth, and BER? Is the performance comparable or inferior to simpler pump-plus-filter approaches? This trade-off needs clarification.
(c) While a 61.5% conversion efficiency for 15 lines is reported, power distribution is uneven. Spectral flattening for power equalization introduces additional insertion loss. The authors should recalculate an "effective" conversion efficiency considering usable lines post-equalization.

3.The manuscript mentions injection-locked amplification as a future improvement but this contradicts earlier claims that such techniques are less suitable for lightweight systems. Furthermore, prior work (e.g., Ref. [22]) has already demonstrated injection-locked amplification of SIL microcombs with comparable or better performance. The authors should re-evaluate their novelty claim and clarify the meaningful differences of their implementation compared to these prior studies.

4. Minor issues and editorial errors:
(a) Line 202: "gray dots" should be "purple dots".
(b) Supplementary Note 4, line 65: "Fig.1(e)" reference is unclear.

accordance with their suggestions. Here, we present a point-by-point reply (in blue) to the reviewers'
comments (in black). All the changes have been highlighted (in red) with corresponding original text

Response to the report from the Referee #1
General comments: "This paper presents the use of a self injection locked microcomb as a source for coherent optical fiber
transmission in the C-band achieving a net rate of 8.4 Tbps in WDM scheme and a net 200 Tbps in a WDM + MCF
configuration. Additionally, MDM transmissions are also demonstrated achieving net 9.57 and 8.37 Tbps. The authors claim
a 10-fold reduction in resource requirements for similar capacity architectures. The paper is well organized but could
improve in the following areas."
Our reply: We are sincerely grateful for the reviewer’s favorable comments on our study. In the revised manuscript, we
have included design and experimental details and carefully proofread the manuscript. Please find our point-by-point
response attached.
Comment 1: "Please specify in more details the exact DSP that was used at both the transmitter and at the receiver. It would
be interesting to know filter lengths, equalization and pre-emphasise used, etc."
Our reply: Thanks for your valuable comment regarding the insufficient description of our experiments. In response, we
have provided a detailed explanation of the DSP aspects:
(Materials and Methods, page 28) In the context of DSP, at the transmitter side, we initially generate a PRBS sequence for
QAM mapping, followed by 0.01 Root Raised Cosine pulse shaping, and then resample the signal before sending it to the
AWG. On the receiver side, the captured signal undergoes sequential processing including resampling, frame
synchronization, dispersion compensation, carrier frequency offset estimation using the fourth-power algorithm, adaptive
MIMO equalization, carrier phase recovery through a two-stage blind phase search algorithm (with filter lengths of 32 and
8 for the first and second stages, respectively), demodulation, and BER calculation. It is noteworthy that during the
verification of the relationship between OCNR and linewidth versus maximum net rate, DSP section utilized an 81-tap
adaptive MIMO equalizer. In other experimental scenarios, the use of a 41-tap MIMO equalizer with reduced compensation
capability and the decreased received OSNR per combline caused by WDM collectively lead to a degradation in achievable
symbol rate compared to the former configuration.
Comment 2: "The authors claim the first coherent single-lambda comb-based transmission results over 1 Tbps, however
their citation [8] (Bernal S, et al.) includes a single-lambda demonstration of 1.6 Tbps in the O-band. Please adapt the claim
accordingly."
Our reply: Thanks for the correction. Indeed, our work does not constitute the first demonstration of an integrated light
source achieving single-carrier 1 Tbps transmission, as we had overlooked prior works in O-band communications. Instead
of claiming single-carrier channel rates, in the revised version, we further demonstrate exceeding 1 Tbps (110 Gbaud DP-
due to their inherent limitations in linewidth and OCNR. We have updated the newly added experiment in Fig. 3(b) and (c)
as follows:
Fig. 3 SMF transmission system. (a) Schematic diagram of the high-speed node-to-node transmission system for short-reach
campus/edge networks and metropolitan-scale optical transmission. (b) The self-homodyne-based campus/edge
interconnect system achieves per-channel transmission rates exceeding 1 Tbps across all wavelength channels. (c)
Constellation diagram of DP-32QAM.
(Introduction, page 6) We simulated short-range campus/edge networks and metropolitan area network transmission
separately. In the campus/edge networks, we achieved a transmission capacity of 1 Tbps/λ across all carriers using a self-
homodyne system.
Comment 3: "The authors compare the performance of the comb lines vs commercial ECLs for different OSNR values. It
would be valuable to add a discussion on the amount of gain needed in their proposed architecture since it requires more
optical amplification than a single laser WDM scheme. "
Our reply: We appreciate these valuable suggestions. A comparative analysis has been added in the revised Supplementary
Information, as shown in the following figure. In summary, the output power of the integrated frequency comb is lower
than that of conventional laser-array-based WDM schemes (assuming 0 dBm output), requiring an additional 13 dB of gain.
While the additional noise influence brought by amplification can be effectively alleviated by the narrow linewidth
characteristic.
Fig. S2 Gain Comparison: SIL Comb vs. Commercial External-Cavity Laser.
(Supplementary Note 3) Here we present a comparative analysis of the gain requirement between the SIL microcomb and
the laser-array schemes. To ensure a fair comparison, the input power to the modulator is fixed at 10 dBm (its optimal
operating point) across all configurations. With higher output power, the system with laser arrays eliminates the need for
the first-stage EDFA (shown in Fig. S2 bottom panel). And the WSS before IQ modulators for demultiplex is not needed. For
the microcomb-based approach, due to the 5 dB insertion loss introduced by the WSS, this scheme requires an additional
13 dB of first-stage gain compensation, with additional OCNR degradation. However, due to the narrow-linewidth
characteristics of the self-injection-locked microcomb, the receiver achieves the same level of BER, despite remaining a 3

(Discussion, page 20) Owing to the high conversion efficiency and coherence of each combline, the highest single channel

level of high-power bulk lasers48. Although the output power of the integrated frequency comb remains lower than that of
traditional bulk laser arrays, this limitation is compensated during transmission by the comb's high conversion efficiency
and narrow linewidth characteristics.

comb, two EDFAs, one WSS, and two DP-IQMs. Based on calculations, the total footprint measures 2300 cm² with a height
of 12 cm in the system, with sizes of each individual components are listed below:
Component Number Volume (cm*cm*cm)
SIL Comb 1 2.8*1.2*1
EDFA 2 32*25*10
WSS 1 31*24*12
DP-IQM 2 8.8*1.4*1
From the above table, the bulky EDFA and WSS occupy the majority of the volume, making the transmitter appear less

16 channels remains challenging, the proposed all-modular system demonstrates that on-chip architectures can sustain
equally high channel rates. This approach simultaneously achieves system miniaturization while meeting inter-node
transmission requirements.
Component Number Volume (cm*cm*cm)
SIL Comb 1 2.8*1.2*1
SOA 2 3*1.27*1
IWC 2 5.2*4.8*3
DP-IQM 2 8.8*1.4*1
Fig. 5 Highly integrated transmitter demonstration. (b) Physical Diagram of the Transmitter Module.

coherent receiver can be implemented, as demonstrated in our previous work [Laser & Photonics Reviews, 18(1): 2300501,
(2024)], with further plans to realize a fully lightweight transceiver link.
(Discussion, page 22) Extending this approach to the receiver side is equally feasible, where the proposed chip-level parallel
optical source can serve as local oscillators in combination with integrated photodetectors and demultiplexers49. The co-
integration of transmitters and receivers would enable a lightweight platform for bidirectional transmission.
Comment 5: "The discussion section provides a good summary of the obtained results as compared to previous works but
does not provide an impactful argument explaining why this type of comb source is ideal for their proposed architecture. A
more detailed comparison between the limitations of this type of comb source compared to others would be of great
interest."
Our reply: Thanks for the valuable insights. Our SIL source indeed offers distinct advantages in terms of the simultaneously
achieved high coherence and OCNR, which ensures parallel high-capacity data transmission in a shrunk form factor
compared with the traditional bulky laser array and other externally pumped comb approach.
In the revised manuscript, we systematically analyze the influence of OCNR and linewidth on the maximum transmission
rate under back-to-back (BTB) conditions, as shown in Fig. 2(e) of the revised manuscript. As seen from the figure, the
higher OCNR and narrower linewidth will result in a higher maximum transmission rate. This is exactly what SIL dark-
pulse microcomb can provide, as we demonstrate in this manuscript. With SIL operation, such parallel sources feature
remarkable narrow linewidth, along with simple operation and fully integrated. In the normal dispersion microresonator,
the mode-locked dark-pulse state is well-known for the high conversion efficiency, experimentally >60% in this manuscript.
Such high conversion efficiency ensures a high single channel power, equivalently a high OCNR. Such unique combination
enables tolerance to higher insertion losses and SNR degradation, especially when employing lossy on-chip WDM devices
and noisy SOAs in a space-constrained scenario.
Compared with other comb sources, semiconductor mode-locked laser chips face inherent phase noise limitations, leading
to wide linewidth of ~1 MHz and blocking high-coherence transmission. Limited by the long cavity length, bulky mode-
locked lasers tend to feature combline spacing < 1 GHz, which require precise filtering to select target comblines for suitable
channel spacing. Conventional microcombs demand the delicate frequency alignment between the pump laser and the
microresonator. In addition, the coherence is determined by the pump laser, where chip-level lasers are insufficient to
provide the pump with both high power and high coherence. Electro-optic combs, while alternative solutions, require
additional microwave drivers with high cost and increased complexity, and the coherence also relies on the external sources.
Fig. 2 Integrated coherent comb source generation and the effect of light source on transmission. (e) The influence of
OCNR and linewidth on the maximum net symbol rate is evaluated under the error-free condition. The red pentagrams in

Fig. 5 Highly integrated transmitter demonstration. (d) Intrinsic linewidth characteristics of individual combline. The black

(Results, page 18) For comparation, we implement a reference system using a 45-GHz-spacing electro-optic frequency comb

(Discussion, page 20) Owing to the high conversion efficiency and coherence of each combline, the highest single channel

(Supplementary Note 5) In integrated WDM transmission systems, light sources exhibit the most significant susceptibility

Fig. S4 The optical spectrum varies with ambient temperature from 21.5°C to 28.5°C, where cross markers in the figure

Response to the report from the Referee #2
General comments: "In this manuscript, “Exploiting a Centrally Powered Coherent Microcomb for Lightweight Optical
Transmission” , the authors use the comb lines of a microcomb to demonstrate:
- 1 Tbps (115 GBd 32 QAM-DP) with one of the lines;
- 8.4 Tbit/s with 16 lines (70 GBd 16QAM-DP) over 160 km of SSMF;
- 200 Tbps with 16 lines (40 GBd 16QAM-DP) over 2 km of a 24-core fiber;
- 9.5 Tbps with 16 lines (40 GBd 16QAM-DP) over 25 km of a 2-mode (LP) fiber;
- 8.4 Tbps with 16 lines (70 GBd 16QAM-SP) over 50 m of a 2-mode (OAM) fiber.
The authors make use of such high symbol rates thanks to the low noise properties of each comb line, which is achieved by
self-injection locking of the DFB pump laser. While the high on-chip conversion efficiency of 60% is associated with the type
of comb.
The manuscript is clearly written, and the topic and results are relevant for the scientific community."
Our reply: We are deeply grateful for the thoughtful evaluation of our work and sincerely appreciate the considerable time
and effort you have dedicated to reviewing our manuscript. All responses to the reviewers' comments and corresponding
manuscript revisions have been clearly documented. Please find our point-by-point response attached.
Comment 1: "My major concern relates to the novelty impact of this work. First, regarding the comb the authors employ,
this seems to be the same as the one reported in Ref. 22, where the noise reduction is already analysed (as well as in other
references) and the comb is already used for data transmission: 30 GBd, 32QAM-DP. The authors, thus need to clarify if this
is the same comb and what is the main novelty with respect to that work. Otherwise, the work feels that it is an incremental
enabled by using better components such as modulators and AWGs."
Our reply: We sincerely appreciate the reviewer's valuable feedback and would like to clarify the key distinctions between
our work and Ref. 22. First, it should be noted that the two studies are based on fundamentally different chip designs (Ref.
22 employs a 100-nm-thick ultra-high Q device, whereas ours employs a 300-nm-thick structure). Below, we systematically
outline the key distinctions of our work:
1. Energy Efficiency: Reference 22 utilizes an add-drop microresonator, with each comb line exhibiting only -20 dBm
output power. In this manuscript, with special over-coupling design, we achieve >60% conversion efficiency, resulting
in exceeding -10 dBm power for each combline.
2. Channel spacing: The 100-nm-thick SiN is hard to get high-Q resonator with larger FSR (>40 GHz). This design choice
inherently limits their capability to support higher-speed signal at each carrier. Based on 300-nm-thick SiN platform, it
is easy to realize high-Q microresonator with large FSR >100 GHz for high single-channel transmission. In our revision,
rather than relying on single-channel demonstrations, we successfully achieved ultra-high data rates using 110-Gbaud
DP-32QAM, corresponding to over 1 Tbps, across all 16 comb lines (Response to Comment 2), which strongly supports
our claims.
3. Cost: Reference 22 intended to realize ultra-low-noise sources. To suppress the phase noise as much as possible, the
prior work adopted the ultra-low-loss photonic circuits based on 100-nm-thick SiN. Such extraordinary platform
requires complete and costly fabrication processes and is difficult to obtain commercially at present. By contrast, the
300-nm-thick SiN is widely available [CUMEC-CSiN300, IMB-CNM & VLC Photonics, LIGENTEC, GLOBALFOUNDRIES],
and the fabrication process is much simpler. This ensures the universality and low cost of this solution.
4. Compactness: Regarding system architecture, Ref. 22 employs multiple DFBs for injection locking, each requiring
individual laser drivers (LD) and thermoelectric cooler (TEC) control, which inherently limits its suitability for
lightweight transmission systems. By contrast, our system fully exploits the inherently high conversion efficiency and
low noise of the designed light source, aiming for greater simplicity than other microcomb based systems. To further
strengthen this claim, in our revised manuscript, we have conducted additional lightweight transmission experiment
by replacing bulky system components with integrated ones, such as SOAs and integrated waveshaping chip (IWC)
for WDM operation (Response to Comment 3). Those compact devices, to the best of our knowledge, have not yet
been simultaneously adopted in other comb-based transmission systems. This integration enables a significantly more
compact transmitter architecture, achieving nearly an 80-fold reduction in system size compared with our previous
demonstration. Even under the noisy SOA amplification and extra insertion loss from the waveshaping chip, the system
still performs a 16 WDM transmission with over 5 Tbps aggregation rate, showing promise in noise tolerance and
compact-system suitability of the proposed light source.
5. Performance analysis with quantified experimental verification: In our newly revised manuscript, to better clarify
how the high OCNR and noise-suppression effect in a comb source affect the transmission results, systematic analysis
has been conducted (Response to Comment 2). The relationship between baud rate and noise-OCNR is experimentally
explored by the substituting light source with different linewidth and varying emission intensity in each of them. The
characterization provides critical insights for future high-coherence transmission experiments.
Comment 2: "Second, when it comes to the 1 Tbps claim, this is shown only for one of the comb lines, i.e., the pump line. The authors
should also characterize other lines in the same way (Fig. 2g). Will there be a penalty due to the lower power / higher noise?
With only one line, their 1 Tbps is not that novel, see ,e.g., [Buchali, 1-Terabit/s Net Data-Rate Transceiver Based on Single-
Carrier Nyquist-Shaped 124 Gbaud PDM-32QAM], or [First Single-Carrier Transmission at Net Data Rates of 1.6 Tb/s over
9075 km and 2.4 Tb/s over 1210 km Using 300 GBd Dual-Polarization Signals and Probabilistic Constellation Shaping]. "
Our reply: Thanks for these valuable comments and questions. In our revised manuscript, to better demonstrate the
transmission potential of a low-noise comb source, we carried out over 1 Tbps data transmission utilizing all 16 high-
power microcomb carriers under a WDM configuration, as shown in the following Fig. 3(a). All channel achieved BER under
7E-3 (Fig. 3(b)). Accordingly, we have added the following description of the new experiments.
(Result, page 11) SIL comblines are divided into odd and even banks to simulate real-world communication scenarios. First,
we build up a 1 km self-hemodyne coherent transmission system to explore the maximum capacity of the comelines.
Limited by the channel spacing of 100 GHz, we artificially doubled the spectral interval through WSS, as shown in Fig. 3(b),
and distinguish by transparency. Thanks to the high OCNR with power levels above -10 dBm, all channels can support 110
GBaud DP-32QAM signal transmissions in the WDM configuration, indicating single-channel rate of 1.1 (net 1.008) Tbps.
Fig. 3 SMF transmission system. (a) Schematic diagram of the high-speed node-to-node transmission system for short-reach
campus/edge networks and metropolitan-scale optical transmission. (b) The self-homodyne-based campus/edge
interconnect system achieves per-channel transmission rates exceeding 1 Tbps across all wavelength channels. (c)
Constellation diagram of DP-32QAM.
In addition, to provide more quantitative experimental evidence of how low OCNR and coherence impact transmission
performance, we performed extensive experimental characterization, as shown in the following Fig. 2(e). To emulate
different conditions, benchtop lasers with varying linewidths were employed, with the OCNR of each laser tuned through
its output power. The results indicate that both high coherence and OCNR are crucial for supporting high transmission
speeds, capabilities that our proposed microcomb inherently offers.
Fig. 2 Integrated coherent comb source generation and the effect of light source on transmission. (e) The influence of
OCNR and linewidth on the maximum net symbol rate is evaluated under the error-free condition. The red pentagrams in
the figure trace the degradation path of the light source in the communication system.
Comment 3: "If the selling point is to also demonstrate the high data rate with MCF, FMF, RCF, there has been already works
bringing this approach tothe extrem: [22.9 Pb/s data-rate by extreme space-wavelength multiplexing] with a few-modes
MCF providing 114 spatial channels (30 Tbps/wavelength)."
Our reply: We are sorry for any misleading in the original manuscript. Actually, this work aims to provide deeper insights
into an ultra-compact microcomb-based transmission system capable of supporting high-capacity links between space-
constrained supernodes of computing units. Multiplexing techniques such as MCF, FMF, and RCF represent potential
solutions for enabling multi-node aggregation in transmission networks. Here, we demonstrate that a lightweight
transmission system based on a self-injection-locked microcomb source can be organized in this manner.
We thank the reviewer for stimulating our consideration of the key selling points of this work. To further substantiate the
“lightweight” claim, we propose a chip-level transmitter by replacing bulky components with integrated ones, such as
SOAs and integrated waveshaping chips (IWCs) for WDM operation, as shown in Fig. 5(a–c). The results demonstrate per-
channel data rates exceeding 320 Gbps, with an aggregate capacity of over 5 Tbps, as shown in Fig. 5(e). Moreover, the
high conversion efficiency and narrow linewidth of the proposed SIL microcomb source play a critical role in mitigating the
degradation induced by additional noise of integrated devices. As analyzed in Fig. 5(f–g), compared with commercial EDFAs,
SOA amplification introduces more severe frequency noise and OSNR degradation, yet the SIL microcomb exhibits strong
resilience against these impairments.
Fig. 5 Highly integrated transmitter demonstration. (a) Lightweight Transmitter Scheme. (b) Physical Diagram of the

(Result, page 17) A highly integrated system is essential for realizing lightweight transmission in distributed edge nodes,
especially under stringent cost and footprint constraints. In this section, beyond integrated light sources, we present a chip-
level parallel carrier generator where bulky WSSs and EDFAs are replaced by SOAs and silicon photonic IWCs. Figure 5(a)
illustrates the architecture of the chip-level transmitter module, with photographs of all modules provided in Fig. 5(b). The
IWC is fabricated using mature silicon photonics technology, featuring cascaded microring resonators with a free spectral
range (FSR) of approximately 1.3 THz. Microheaters placed above the microrings allow tuning of resonant frequencies to
adjust the output spectrum, as detailed in Supplementary Information Note 5. To suppress thermal crosstalk, adjacent
microrings are physically separated by etched trenches, as illustrated in Fig. 5(c). Since not all comblines require power
equalization, we achieve uniform power distribution across all spectral lines using only 12 microrings. After the IWC, all 16
comblines are equalized to -18 dBm, accounting for an 8 dB insertion loss. The carriers are then amplified by an SOA and
routed through another IWC for odd-even channel separation. Separated carriers are modulated by 35-GHz-bandwidth IQ
modulators, combined, and then amplified through an SOA before transmission. As demonstrated in Fig. 5(e), a 10-km
transmission at 5.12 Tbps (net 5.015 Tbps) is achieved using 40-GBaud DP-16QAM modulation. The BER trend per channel
aligns consistently with the linewidth values as shown in Fig. 5(d), with comblines below 300 Hz linewidth achieving error-
free operation.
It is noteworthy that the capacity of the present chip-level transmitter is lower than that of systems based on bulky devices.
This primarily stems from carrier performance degradation caused by integrated components, which featuring higher noise
figures and insertion losses than their benchtop counterparts. Specifically, the IWC contributes an additional 3 dB insertion
loss compared to benchtop WSS. SOAs, while far more compact than EDFAs, introduce excessive amplified spontaneous
emission (ASE) noise. Meanwhile, their high α-factor and nonlinear effects (notably XPM) further induce cumulative phase
noise and waveform distortion in high-speed systems46,47. Figure 5(f) and (g) present the corresponding noise and OSNR
degradation after amplification. When amplified to 10 dBm, the linewidth of channel 6 increases of approximately threefold
and tenfold via EDFA and SOA respectively. In addition, the OCNR decreases by 6 dB and 12.5 dB respectively. Despite these
impairments, the SIL light source still enables >5 Tbps transmission within the chip-level lightweight system, due to its
original superior coherence and OCNR. For comparation, we implement a reference system using a 45-GHz-spacing electro-
optic frequency comb pumped by an N7714A ECL (Fig. 5(d)). Under identical conditions, severely degraded constellation
diagrams are obtained due to its poor original coherence (Fig. 5(e) black pentagrams).

Comment 6: "The authors highlight the power conversion efficiency, but what about the wall-plug efficiency? How does it
compare to other similar approaches?"
Our reply: Our InP-DFB laser operates with a laser voltage of 1.564 V and current of 300 mA, delivering an output power
of 18 dBm (63.1 mW). The wall-plug efficiency (WPE) is calculated as: 63.1/469.2 = 13.45%.
This performance falls within a relatively ideal range (9-16%) [Opt. Express 30, 27983-27992 (2022)]. The primary
limitations come from the laser's intrinsic quantum efficiency as well as optical losses caused by reflection and absorption.

WPE and power conversion efficiency [Journal of Lightwave Technology 38, 5517-5525 (2020)], our design demonstrates
a clear superiority (inferred ~18 dB). We have now included this information in the main text.
(Result, page 9) A laser diode chip, which exhibits a wall-plug efficiency of 13.45%, is directly coupled with the designed
silicon nitride (SiN) microresonator chip.

Response to the report from the Referee #3
General comments: "This manuscript reports technically work demonstrating high-speed multidimensional optical
communication utilizing a self-injection-locked (SIL) dark-pulse microcomb. The authors ascribe the achieved high baud rate
and 1 Tbps per-channel performance to the noise suppression facilitated by injection locking. However, in comparison with
existing literature, this study does not introduce a fundamentally novel device architecture or a system-level innovation of
transformative significance. Rather, the primary contribution appears to be the enhancement of single-carrier transmission
rates, achieved at the cost of a reduced number of utilized channels, without providing substantial forward-looking
perspectives. Consequently, I believe the scope and impact of this work might be more appropriately aligned with the focus
of specialized journals in photonics or communications. The reasons I'm not entirely convinced by this work are listed below."
Our reply: We sincerely appreciate the reviewers' valuable comments. Here, we would like to further elaborate on the
significance and innovative aspects of our work. We have provided a detailed, point-by-point response to clarify the
technical aspects and address all raised concerns. We also conducted additional experiments to further support our claims.
First of all, we would like to clarify that our work specifically addresses the communication and aggregation challenges
among distributed edge computing nodes [1]. In such scenarios, an excessive number of wavelength channels imposes
significant pressure on hardware components. Our primary goal is to develop a lightweight parallel transmission system,
with reduced volume, power consumption and cost, to meet the growing high-capacity demands of network edges and
modular data centers in space-constrained scenarios.
We understand the reviewer's concerns mainly focus on three aspects:
(1) First, the reason why such a comb source could support superior transmission lacked quantitative support, and the
differences from previous work were not specified in detail.
(2) Second, our emphasized single-carrier rate transmission capability comes at the cost of reduced channel count. The
presentation of parallelism is insufficient.
(3) Third, the system is not "lightweight" enough, as some components such as WSS and EDFA cannot be modularized,
which contradicts the lightweight architecture.
For (1): We conducted additional experiments to quantify the relationship between the maximum transmission rate and
OCNR and linewidth of the laser carrier. The results demonstrate that the high coherence and high conversion efficiency
of our light source strongly support such high-speed transmission. (Response to Comment 1). In the revised main text,
newly added Fig. 2(e) presents such relationship. Moreover, the superior coherence and OCNR provide strong resilience
against amplification-induced degradation, allowing the system to tolerate the additional noise introduced by SOAs when
replacing bulky EDFAs, thereby enabling a more compact configuration. Supplementary experiments are also performed as
in newly added Fig. 5 for analysis on such impact.
In comparison, none of the currently available integrated optical frequency combs (typically featuring around 10 kHz
linewidth and 40 dB OCNR) could reach such performance while remaining compact. Also, compared to previous work
(e.g., Ref. 22), our design achieves significantly improved integration simplicity. In terms of device architecture, we reduced
components by removing additional LDs and TEC controllers, as we require only a single DFB pump. Regarding power
efficiency, our design achieves higher conversion efficiency compared to prior solutions. Most importantly, Ref. 22 primarily
aimed to realize an integrated ultra-low-noise parallel source, which required ultra-low-loss integrated photonic circuits
(thin SiN). Such platforms are costly and difficult to obtain commercially. At the system level, we obtained remarkable
transmission results - achieving 200 Tbps using just 16 comblines. This demonstration breaks the conventional paradigm
by scaling up the capacity of each channel in a micro-parallelism system with low system overhead, rather than scaling up
channel numbers with relatively low per-channel data rates.
For (2): We firmly believe that enhancing single-carrier rates holds significant value - indeed, this represents a critical
performance metric where integrated optical frequency combs currently lag behind bulk laser systems [2,3]. As mentioned
before, an excessive number of comblines does not necessarily translate to practical advantages, especially in resource-
constrained scenarios. Through innovative microring resonator design, we achieve more concentrated energy distribution
within targeted spectral regions (as elaborated in the Supplementary Information). While our initial single-carrier 1 Tbps
transmission is indeed lack convincement, in the revised manuscript, we have substantiated our approach by
demonstrating uniform 1 Tbps transmission (110 Gbaud DP-32QAM) across all 16-comblines (Fig. 3(b)) (Response to
Comment 1-c). Implemented via our self-homodyne architecture, this solution unlocks the potential of ultrahigh per-
channel rate parallel transmission, making it well-suited for short-reach campus and edge network environments with
stringent bandwidth demands.
For (3): We performed a proof-of-concept lightweight transmission link, by replacing the bulk WSSs and EDFAs with
integrated waveshaping chips and semiconductor optical amplifiers, in the revised manuscript. By leveraging integrated
photonic devices, the system volume is reduced by 80-fold. We find that such replacement degrade both the carrier
linewidth and the received OSNR. However, thanks to its high carrier power and narrow linewidth, the SIL microcomb
exhibits significantly high tolerance to both OSNR degradation and coherence impairment. Comparative experiments are
also conducted with EO combs, which further confirm that the proposed SIL microcomb source can withstand such
degradation (Response to Comment 2).
In conclusion, this work introduces both the concept and the first practical demonstration of a chip-level lightweight optical
transmission system. It represents a paradigm shift toward greener, higher-density compute-and-transport architectures,
with broad potential impact across fields such as high-performance computing and intelligent manufacturing. To address
the novelty concerns raised by reviewers, we have substantially revised the manuscript and added three compelling new
experiments. We hope that the responses provided below fully address the reviewer’s concerns. We sincerely thank the
reviewer for their thorough and thoughtful review.
